headline: Daily Start app opens your to-do list automatically each morning
summary: This new open-source app built with Electron aims to solve forgetfulness by proactively displaying your daily checklist at a set time.
details: Tired of forgetting your to-do list? The new Daily Start app is designed to combat this by automatically opening your checklist at a scheduled time each morning.
The app, built with Electron, stores your data locally on your computer, ensuring your checklist remains private and accessible directly by you.
Daily Start aims to be a simple productivity tool, avoiding the complexity of larger platforms. It's free, open-source, and available for Windows 10 and 11.
The app features a 'daily check-in' that only needs to be responded to once. If you close the window, it will reappear shortly to ensure you engage with your tasks.
It also includes templates for quickly answering frequently asked questions or storing reusable snippets, streamlining your workflow.

headline_marked: [[Florida driver data]] published by hackers after state database breach
headline: Florida driver data published by hackers after state database breach
summary: Thousands of vehicle ownership certificates and some personal documents were leaked after a hacking group breached the state's DAVID database.
details: The ShinyHunters hacking group has published hundreds of thousands of files from a Florida state database of vehicles and driver information. The hackers stated the data was released because the victim did not pay a ransom or cooperate with their demands.
The breach targeted the DAVID database earlier in September. As evidence, the hackers posted a screenshot that appeared to be a record associated with Jeffrey Epstein, who had a residence in Florida.

The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV) confirmed a data breach occurred after hackers obtained credentials from a police officer stored on a personal device. The agency has not yet commented on the published data.

The stolen data includes hundreds of thousands of vehicle ownership certificates with names and addresses of buyers and sellers, as well as vehicle identification numbers. A smaller subset of files contained Social Security numbers and other government-issued documents like non-U.S. passports and immigration papers.
This incident follows a major hack at identity verification company IDScan, which resulted in the theft of over 150 million images of driver's licenses.
